question: What value of label smoothing did the Transformer authors use during training?
answer:

question: How many identical layers make up the Transformer's encoder stack?
answer:
The Transformer's encoder stack is composed of a stack of N = 6 identical layers [Attention Is All You Need, p.3]. Each of these layers contains two sub-layers [Attention Is All You Need, p.3]. This structure is part of the overall architecture that uses stacked self-attention and point-wise, fully connected layers for both the encoder and decoder [Attention Is All You Need, p.3].

question: Why do the Transformer authors scale the dot products by 1/sqrt(dk)?
answer:
[[ANSWER]]
The authors scale the dot products by $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ to counteract the effect of large $d_k$ values causing dot products to grow large in magnitude [Attention Is All You Need, p.4]. This growth pushes the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients [Attention Is All You Need, p.4]. Scaling prevents this issue, ensuring stable training [Attention Is All You Need, p.4].

question: How many warmup steps does the Transformer's learning rate schedule use?
answer:
The Transformer's learning rate schedule uses 4000 warmup steps [Attention Is All You Need, p.7]. This corresponds to increasing the learning rate linearly for the first 4000 training steps, after which it decreases proportionally to the inverse square root of the step number [Attention Is All You Need, p.7].

question: What BLEU score did the big Transformer reach on WMT 2014 English-to-German?

question: What are Moshi's theoretical and practical latencies?
answer:
Moshi has a theoretical latency of 160ms [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, p.26][Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, p.1]. In practice, its latency is 200ms [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, p.1]. The theoretical latency is achieved by pretraining with an acoustic delay of 2 and finetuning with an acoustic delay of 1 [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, p.26].

question: By what factor does H-Net improve data efficiency on DNA modelling compared with isotropic models?
answer:
H-Net improves data efficiency on DNA modeling by a factor of 3.6 compared to isotropic models [Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling, p.4]. This improvement is consistent across multiple sections, where each H-Net model achieves the same predecay perplexity as the corresponding isotropic model with approximately 3.6× less data [Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling, p.17]. Additionally, ablation studies confirm that H-Net (1-stage) with an M3T1 encoder achieves 3.6× the data efficiency of an isotropic architecture [Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling, p.37].
